PRODSECRM-306.summary: Slow recovery from signing key compromise
PRODSECRM-306.description:
Risk Type: Operational
Risk Level: Product Security level
Team: PSRD
Severity: Moderate
Likelihood: Unlikely
Proximity: Long term - < 1 month
Category: Release
Specific Risk:
Situation
Every RPM package shipped by RHEL is signed with one of Red Hat’s release package signing keys, currently a 4096-bit RSA key “release2”, and an ML-DSA-87 & Ed448 key “release4”. These keys are kept in hardware security modules (HSMs) which do not allow export, but do allow using the keys to create signatures. These keys are long-lived: we do not have a fixed rotation schedule for them.
Our RPM delivery pipeline does not allow for the contents of a specific RPM file — identified by the tuple of name, version, revision (NVR) — to change once it has shipped. Recently such cases were inadvertently triggered by the transition to post-quantum cryptography signatures on modular RPMs, and have caused issues in pulp, the CDN, and a large number of customer cases.
The only way to sign RPMs with new keys is to rebuild the package from source with an increased revision field and push it through the delivery pipeline.
Background
The RHEL delivery pipeline has many steps. These are loosely:
RHEL JIRA ticket
Change in the RPM .spec file
GitLab pull request & CI run
Merge & Build
Test execution & QA
Release through Errata Tool
Just the time required to build, test, and ship a new package (i.e., starting at step 4) is already prohibitively long: for all builds targeting z-stream in RHEL 10, the observed median hang time after the build was started is 13.7 days, the 90th percentile is 51.3 days, the 99th percentile is 111.8 days. Even if we assume that the rebuilds would be the highest priority, the 10th percentile is still 2d 21h. There would be a massive load on our build and test infrastructure. A number of packages would likely fail to build from source due to bitrot, time bombs in test artifacts, changes in dependencies and the buildroot, or other similar issues. Teams couldn’t rebuild all packages in parallel due to limited compute and engineering capacity. It would feel like every single package we ship would — at the same time — be hit with a critical CVE.
I did file https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHELDST-43646#icft=RHELDST-43646
 to request changing the delivery pipeline to support changes in RPMs — such as their signatures — without rebuilding. From the discussion in the comments so far, it seems this may affect a number of different parts.
We could also work around this issue by changing the revision field of existing RPMs and then re-signing the modified copies without rebuilding from source, essentially skipping steps 1-4 above. Because of dependencies between RPMs that would have to be adjusted, this would have to be custom tooling to work on an entire repository. Unless we also run through steps 5 and 6 from above, this approach has a higher risk of unexpected problems and inconsistencies (e.g., the modified revision-bumped RPMs potentially missing from the customer portal).
The Post-Quantum Cryptography Program is facing a problem originating in the same root cause: RHEL cannot re-sign all of its existing packages with post-quantum signatures to achieve a fully PQ-signed distribution without planning, tracking, and executing a full rebuild of every package. If the rebuild was not necessary to re-sign packages with new keys, a PQ-signed RHEL would be achievable much quicker, and with less effort.
Potential Impact:
Assessment
A note on probability
A breach of our signing servers or infrastructure with access to signing servers is very unlikely, and even if a breach happens, the raw key material cannot be exported from the hardware security modules, i.e., an attacker could only use their illicit access to sign a few RPMs of their own. However, we do not have a revocation mechanism for signed RPMs, so if we end up in a situation where we cannot determine which forged RPMs were signed, or there are too many to ask customers to explicitly blocklist them, a key rotation is the only sensible path for recovery.
Impact
Should we end up in a situation where we need to rotate the key and re-sign existing releases, it is my assessment that we will not be able to complete that activity in a reasonable amount of time as our customers would expect.
We can not re-sign existing built RPMs and push them out because it breaks our delivery pipeline if the contents of an RPM change, but its file name does not.
I estimate that it would take us about a month to rebuild all packages in the current RHEL 10 z-stream from source and get them shipped, due to the length of the delivery pipeline as explained above. We would not only have to rebuild RHEL 10, though; all other still supported releases would equally have to be rebuilt from source.
Being unable to address CVEs or any other customer requests for RHEL for at least a month would generate a massive amount of bad press and burn goodwill. We would almost certainly lose customers and be subject to various inquiries and investigations.
Combining likelihood and impact
The likelihood of this happening is low. The damage should it happen is excessively large. The expected value of damages, calculated from the probability of an event multiplied by the impact, is hard to estimate because of uncertainty in the likelihood.
Options
There are multiple options to handle this risk:
Accept it: if we deem the probability low enough, the size of the impact does not matter as much.
Improve it from RHEL’s end: make the RHEL delivery pipeline faster and smoother, improve infrastructure stability, and optimize for quicker turnaround times. Start tracking delivery hang times, and create a team with a mandate to improve them. This would also help other goals, e.g., faster CVE fixes.
Build tooling to bump the revision of all latest versions of each package in an RPM repository, then re-sign and deliver those. From a pure dnf/rpm/repository point of view, this can work. We would likely have to run through parts of our delivery pipeline with this approach (i.e., at least Errata Tool). A fast path for unchanged content could speed up delivery, but would need to be built.
Remove the restrictions in the delivery pipeline that force us to never modify existing RPMs, by prioritizing https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHELDST-43646#icft=RHELDST-43646
 and identifying other components that make this assumption and need to be fixed.
Recommendation
I recommend option 4, prioritizing https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHELDST-43646#icft=RHELDST-43646
 and starting an investigation into which other parts of our delivery pipeline need changes to reach this goal. Satellite, for example, might make assumptions on the immutability of a specific RPM file when mirroring RHEL content for disconnected environments. From my point of view, this is the cheapest and quickest path to address the problem, and would also help out the PQC program by opening up a quicker path to an all-PQ-signed RHEL. The Software Production Pipeline team and the Satellite team would be the experts to determine the next steps and assess the cost of this.
Option 2, i.e., improvements of the RHEL delivery pipeline would benefit more than just this problem and are therefore always a good investment. They are, however, likely not the simplest solution for this particular issue.
We should consider working on option 3 in parallel until option 4 is fully implemented. If we need to rotate a key without having implemented any of the other improvements, it would still allow us to react quicker. Not skipping the delivery pipeline will mean we either need a fast path through it, or accept slower deliveries, though.
Existing Mitigation:
none

comments.author: Daniel Alley
comments.body:
It’s worth separating out the various issues.
One issue is kind of fundamental.  If any tool, be that DNF or Satellite, has a cached copy of existing metadata, and files change in-place on a remote location, then the checksums therein will be invalidated and clients will experience errors until they refresh that repo and obtain a fresh copy of the metadata.  In an emergency situation that’s probably an acceptable amount of churn despite customers being exposed to some pain temporarily.  But there’s really no way around it, only mitigations to prevent it from cascading into larger issues, i.e. making sure the copies of packages that are intended to be distributed via the CDN are the ones that actually are present on the CDN, and making sure users of Satellite and other consumers of the repos have a way to forcibly-refresh any impacted repos without an inordinate amount of pain.
Another issue is that, currently, (as best I can tell from the discussions and my slowly decaying historical knowledge of Pulp 2), rhsm-pulp doesn’t have any safeguards on adding a package to a repo which is the same version, but different than, an existing package in the repo, so both co-exist and the resulting conflicts cause serious issues for downstream consumers and require manual cleanup.  That is addressed by https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHELDST-37824
 which should at least prevent that situation from happening accidentally.

Another issue is that, should a mass-resign event be necessary, the restriction that https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHELDST-37824?xpis=eyJicmlkZ2UiOiJzbWFydExpbmtzIiwiaWQiOiIxNzg1NTE2MDIyOTkzIiwic291cmNlIjoiamlyYS1KU1cifQ%3D%3D
 puts in place doesn’t help - so there needs to be a way to replace existing packages within repositories, without much manual effort, while continuing to assert that within a repository there can be only one physical package per each NVRA.  Pulp 3 does this for example: depending on configuration, a repo can either disallow re-adding an NVRA that already exists, or allow adding the NVRA while automatically removing the old one and asserting that only one package exists per NVRA as a final safeguard.  The tooling needs to enforce correct state and not require massive manual checks and cleanup even when the standard safeguard (not allowing the addition of a duplicate at all) is disabled.

And then if there are any issues with the storage of the files on the CDN, that would be separate, but I don’t know enough about that to comment.

comments.author: Clemens Lang
comments.body:
@Daniel Alley 
If any tool, be that DNF or Satellite, has a cached copy of existing metadata, and files change in-place on a remote location, then the checksums therein will be invalidated and clients will experience errors until they refresh that repo and obtain a fresh copy of the metadata.

Yes, that will be a problem, but I think we can also find workarounds for these problems if we look at the entire chain. For example, typically RPM repos are structured in a way where the URL wouldn’t change if the contents of an RPM changes but the NVR does not. Random example: Fedora 44’s latest version of the 0ad package is in on the mirrors atPackages/0/0ad-0.28.0-2.fc44.aarch64.rpm. That is, however, convention, and not a necessity. We could just as well structure the repository in a way where we store packages at Packages/{sha256(package)[0:1]}/{sha256(package)}/package-nvr.rpm, i.e., Packages/45/451c126703d4e3492ff47f5bb0c34f876ea7d12e201d1741c45f34ca62a64efc/0ad-0.28.0-2.fc44.aarch64.rpm such that outdated metadata does not lead to a download failure.
That would likely need changes in https://github.com/rpm-software-management/createrepo_c
, which I believe is what everybody uses to create these, but I don’t think that’s impossible.
Including the hash (or parts of it) of a package in its URL would also fix potential caching and/or freshness problems with the CDN and not require a force refresh, at the cost of doubling the required storage (at least temporarily) should we decide to re-sign the entire archive.

RHELDST-43646.description:
This is a follow-up feature request for https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHELDST-37824
.
While introducing signatures over RPMs with post-quantum cryptography signing keys, we noticed that we could not re-sign existing NVRs — and thereby changing their contents — without violating the assumptions built into pulp, our CDN, and possibly a range of other tools (e.g., Satellite).
I believe the inability to handle this situation gracefully is a problem, so I am filing this feature request to track removal of this limitation: Pulp (and the other tooling we use to deliver RPMs to customers) should support changing the contents of existing NVRs.
Here’s why:
- Due to this limitation, we cannot add post-quantum cryptography signatures to an existing set of RPMs without rebuilding them from source. A RHEL-wide rebuild of all components is a major effort, not only because of the need to track which packages have already been built and the overhead to get all developers to actually do this work, but also because of the engineering time this binds in creating those builds — fixing any compilation issues that might arise — and shepherding them through our delivery pipeline. This delays the point where we can claim the entire set of RPMs has been signed with PQC, and therefore the point where we can require the presence of these signatures and be actually protected against quantum computer attacks by at least a year, but more likely two years.

- This limitation is a major risk in case of key compromise. Rather than generating and distributing a new key, and re-signing our existing archive (which can be done within days), disaster recovery now involves rebuilding all still supported RHEL RPMs (in all versions, major, minor, and EUS) from source. If everything went smoothly, this alone would be gargantuan effort that will take months to pull off. Many of these RPMs, especially the older ones, will however fail to build from source against newer composes, e.g., because a dependency was updated and removed a function declaration from a header but not a library, or because compilers were updated to be more strict in the meantime. In summary: In the event of a key compromise, recovery would take months. This would lead to a significant loss of trust and reputation among our customer base.

I realize this isn’t simple to pull off, and won’t be done yesterday. It will require coordination with other products and projects, e.g., Satellite. It may require changing the way we store files on the CDN, e.g., by switching to content-based addressing (i.e., including the sha256 of a particular artifact in its URL). It’s a major effort, but I believe it is also the correct thing to do to avoid the risk around compromise recovery.

RHELDST-42989.description:
What this is about?
Currently in rhsm-pulp we don’t care about any other signature than the GPG one in RPM - that became problematic when IMA and PQC signing was enabled for RPM content: when a re-signed RPM (with IMA and PQC) of the same NVR was uploaded and associated to production repos - during publish a collision manifested because of the cdn_path (path to origin) of the original RPM was identical to the re-signed RPM. When such repo was published and user tried to consume it, mismatches in checksum typically happened because of that and repo became broken. We want to further improve processing and storing RPMs with multiple signatures so repositories don’t get broken. 
Goal 1 - improve cdn_path (origin) for (S)RPM units:
Currently the cdn_path is created from following components:
/content/origin/rpms/<NAME>/<VERSION>/<RELEASE>/<SIGNING_KEY>/<FILENAME>
https://github.com/release-engineering/pubtools-pulp/blob/69942e537513575df7f8dd58f89c076ca14a94c6/src/pubtools/_pulp/tasks/push/items/rpm.py#L72
  
Problem is that e.g. for ErrataSource we get only the GPG key id from rpm header and we don’t do anything for IMA or PQC keys. 
In order to correctly store RPMs with multiple keys the <SIGNING_KEY>  part of path needs to be different for such RPM.
This needs to correctly work for all pushsource backends. 

Goal 2 - make rhsm-pulp IMA and PQC aware (if needed)
Similar to goal 1, but directly in rhsm-pulp when any RPM is uploaded to rhsm-pulp, the signing_key field is set to short GPG key id which is read from RPM headers and validated during import. Again we don’t care about any other signing keys - so this part should investigate how to make rhms-pulp IMA and PQC aware and whether this really is needed. I believe the signing_key is used only during import for validation (importer on repository holds allowed_keys ) and likely doesn’t have any other usage - but it needs to be reviewed.
The signing_key needs to be set correctly for RPM upload and also for repository sync (whenever (S)RPM unit is created).
If implemented fully, the allowed_keys value on importers needs to be updated.
Goal 3 - add support for re-signed RPMs
Currently we allow to associate RPM to repository with already existing RPM with the NVR but different checksum - this unfortunately hits a problem due to cdn_path collision (Goal 1).
We would like to support such scenario - so while a presence of the same NVR isn’t problematic in pulp repository in general, publishing such repository will create unusable repository (checksum mismatch problem). There are likely multiple way how to solve this:
- when associating to a repository with yum distributor, remove the old duplicate

- when publishing a repository with duplicates - skip the old dupes and and publish only with the most recent RPMs

- … 

In rhsm-pulp there are functions that could take care of that - remove_repo_duplicate_nevra in pulp_rpm repo but it’s currently unknown whether we can use it safely for production repositories.
There is also a couple open questions:
- would be OK to do just “fast-forward” publish when skipping or removing some RPMs? Or would force publish required in this case?

- is exodus tooling fine with this scenario as we do in-place update of a file and we don’t purge cache for this kind of files by default? (may https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Content-addressable_storage
  be a way how to handle that?)


Acceptance criteria:
- investigate possible solutions for goals 1-3

- let RHELDST or any other interested parties review and discuss the proposal

- file follow-up JIRAs

Isn’t that a problem, though? I thought a package changing checksum but keeping filename causes problems for Satellite and other methods to sync copies of our CDN.
However, the behavior you describe would actually be better for us, iff it doesn’t cause any problems — because that would put us in a position where we could re-sign existing NEVRAs with a new key, e.g., in response to a key compromise or to switch to an all-PQC-signed repository.

comments.author: Robert Bikar
comments.body:
@Daniel Alley  @Clemens Lang 
In theory it may work, but there are at least 2 problems:
- in rhsm-pulp (pulp2), we don’t support or care about new type of signing keys (IMA, PQC) so even if we do the replacement of RPM in one repository, in reality it would become a problem for another repository that shares the RPM with the same NVR because it would point to the replaced RPM (and any repo ops would fail with mismatches of checksums)

- the replacement functionality would incur in-place update on CDN which would need extra care (flushing the cache), historically we take rpms as immutable files.

comments.author: Daniel Alley
comments.body:
@Robert Bikar Right, in-place update is bad regardless of how it’s handled, because of caching and other reasons, but there are still better and worse ways of handling it.  I think either blocking it outright or doing a proper swap would be better than silently allowing dups, though I would guess probably blocking it is preferred most of the time.

I was responding mostly to this:

Note: This is not classified as a "bug" because there have been several instances/workflows which previously supported resigning builds in place (producing these duplicate uploads), to the point where we have an established process for cleaning up these builds (though this previously occurred on stage or in Beta repos, where it didn't affect customers). Thus, it should likely be possible to toggle this feature on/off (at the repo level) so that it is still possible to upload duplicate RPMs to a certain set of repos (e.g., repos on stage), if required by certain workflows.

Which I took to mean that there would still be scenarios in which in-place replacement would be done and to which all of those problems still apply, just with additional manual cleanup required.  And I think minimizing those manual interventions and automating the “stay in a correct state” path would still be a good idea.

comments.author: Clemens Lang
comments.body:
@Robert Bikar I’d argue that we should try to address these problems somehow and enable changing files eventually — at the moment, a compromise of our signing keys would mean that we’d have to rebuild every single component in RHEL from source, which I estimate to be a multi-month effort (some components will no longer build from source with updated dependencies or compilers, some components will trigger many test failures that engineers will have to walk through, plus it already takes us >= two weeks to ship a RHEL package). That’s far too slow to do in an incident response situation, and we should have a path to just re-sign the existing contents with a new key and re-publish them. The risk of key compromise is of course low, but if it does happen and we can’t remediate quickly, this may well cost us a significant share of our customers to the point that it becomes an existential risk to our business. If we could change the checksum of existing NEVRAs on the CDN, a much quicker response plan could be created.
Note that this is a long-term thing to address, and the solution to this specific ticket may well look different. I will, however, eventually be bringing up this risk to the RHEL program management, and from there it will probably bubble up further, so consider this a heads-up.

comments.author: Robert Bikar

@Clemens Lang yeah, I understand your concerns, but implementation of such functionality has to be carefully investigated as it may have currently unknown implications. You can file RFE to our project which will definitely help with prioritization and following discussions.

RHELDST-37824.description:
It is currently possible to upload a "duplicate RPM" to pulp. This often occurs when an RPM has been resigned, which changes its checksum, but retains its identifier (NEVRA). This is known to break repositories, and requires a complicated clean up process that generates numerous customer cases.
Note: This is not classified as a "bug" because there have been several instances/workflows which previously supported resigning builds in place (producing these duplicate uploads), to the point where we have an established process for cleaning up these builds (though this previously occurred on stage or in Beta repos, where it didn't affect customers). Thus, it should likely be possible to toggle this feature on/off (at the repo level) so that it is still possible to upload duplicate RPMs to a certain set of repos (e.g., repos on stage), if required by certain workflows.

comments.author: Clemens Lang
comments.body:
Note that the only reason this worked so far was that we were using a deterministic signature scheme, but that was an implementation detail that we should never have relied on. There are probabilistic signature schemes that would have caused the checksum to change with every re-signature, e.g., RSA-PSS, or ECDSA, and the post-quantum signature schemes are also probabilistic.
As a consequence, this can't just be as simple as "re-sign everything on 9.7 or later", it needs to be "sign everything that does not have a signature yet", otherwise we'll see the same problem again when re-shipping 9.7 module content in 9.8 and it gets re-signed with a new ML-DSA signature.

comments.body:
I am in full agreement that we should not re-sign an artifact that already has a signature.
In the past when we had to re-sign an already-shipped artifact, it was an emergency exception that required manual intervention to remove the old artifact from storage and replace it with a new artifact, manually update metadata, etc., and it was extremely messy, error-prone, and time intensive. These are extreme cases where leaving the artifact with the old signature had such a large customer impact that it was deemed it was necessary to do this manual intervention. 
IMO, we still need an exception required for these rare cases that would involve a human review of the customer impact before proceeding. A tool should not be re-signing artifacts as a normal workflow.

Just trying to share a bit more clarity on how the signing server works: The signing server does not know what an Errata is, it just gets a request to sign some RPM (usually from RADAS) and it signs whatever it's told to sign.

comments.author: Clemens Lang
comments.body:
There are two ways to address this: either the signing server recognizes that a signature is already present and does nothing, or the party that sends the signing request just doesn't send it when the package is already signed.
Since the signing server probably doesn't know whether a package has ever shipped out to a customer, and there are limited but legitimate cases where we want to force a re-signature, it feels to me as if the signing server isn't the right place to add this logic, and it should be on the system that sends the signing request to just skip that.

comments.body:
It's not resigning reused component builds that is the problem per se. It's resigning already shipped builds. We're seeing this is reused module components because they are routinely part of multiple errata over time, but any case where where we re-sign and re-push an rpm will hit this problem.

either the signing server recognizes that a signature is already present and does nothing, or the party that sends the signing request just doesn't send it when the package is already signed

An “already signed” check is not exactly what we want. An rpm could be already signed with just the release2 key, but never shipped. In that case, it is fine to re-sign with release4+, and most likely what we want.

Making this decision falls at a data intersection point – errata tool data, brew signature data, publication data in pulp. It seems to me that the logic should probably fall in ET. This is the tool that asks for the specific signatures from radas, and it already deals with data coming from many different sources. In this case, it should recognize that this is a reshipment of an rpm and it should use the same signature as before. 

The other place we might be able to address this is in pulp. This is the tool where the error is after all. I’m a bit surprised that pulp can’t handle this. What if we need to resign an entire product one day for technical or security reasons?

comments.author: Michal Haluza
comments.body:
In the legacy pipeline, it's perfectly valid to have the same build signed by multiple keys. This was done intentionally in the pre-RHEL-7 era, when some products had their own signing keys. Whenever the same build or RPMs were released across multiple products, they were signed multiple times, separately for each product. Early RHEL-ALT for ARM did that. Both Brew and Pulp can handle these scenarios to some extent. Nowadays, we don't see this as often, and we reuse the same signing key for virtually all products, although this is not guaranteed. E.g. RHIVOS uses packages from RHEL and only happens to use the same signing key by coincidence (and possibly some foresight).
Which key should be used for which release is entirely in purview of the Errata Tool or the component that is expected to replace it in Konflux. RADAS does not and should not care about the releases, it should only sign the requested build with the requested keys.
I don't think the fix https://gitlab.cee.redhat.com/errata-guild/errata-rails/-/merge_requests/560 solves the core problem, but it's "good enough" for the legacy pipeline and prevents the module re-signing that we currently have to deal with.
I think the proper fix should have the following logic:
- The Errata Tool has a configuration for signing keys that is a list, and a default signing key, similar to how the brew tags are configured in ET nowadays ("Brew Tags" vs. "Default Brew Tag").

- The releases are configured to use e.g. "release4,release2,ima" by default and an additional "release2" in the permitted signing keys.

- Whenever a build is attached, ET checks to see if it is signed by any of the permitted keys. If so, ET doesn't ask RADAS to re-sign it. If the build isn't signed by any of the permitted keys, ET asks RADAS to sign it using the default signing key. 

All that however works only until someone intentionally requests RADAS to re-sign the build. For that reason, we're also planning to implement a solution in Pulp that considers all signing components (GPG, IMA, and PQC) during upload (see https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHELDST-42989
). This should prevent the duplication of content that occurs today when the GPG component is the same. However not even that solves the problem fully in case someone attempts to upload the same NVR signed by different keys to the same repo, and manual action will likely be always needed in such case.

RHELWF-14251.description:
The signing server applies PQC signatures to all modular RPMs in an advisory, including inherited packages that were previously shipped without PQC signatures.
While modular advisories typically inherit RPMs from previous releases, these "static" packages are being re-signed and reshipped under the same NEVRA. This causes signature/checksum mismatches for packages already present in RHEL repositories. Only the updated RPMs in the advisory should receive the new PQC signatures.
For example: https://errata.devel.redhat.com/advisory/159692 
tmlcoch also provided his assessment of the situation:
I assume that with modules & introduction of PQC, the problem is that the signing logic doesn't account that modules (by default) re-use RPMs from previous module version(s). That said, when a new version of a module is attached to an advisory, that particular module may contain majority of RPMs that we have already shipped long ago - i.e. we shipped them without PQC signatures and only one or few of the RPMs in the module may be actually freshly build (and suitable for PQC signing).
I believe the simple solution for now on the signing logic would be in case of modules to check for "redhatrelease2" key and if that signature exists for the modular RPM then do not proceed with the PQC signing (and just assume it's an RPM we have already shipped before so PQC signing would cause exactly what this jira is about).

Please prevent automatic PQC re-signing of inherited (non-updated) modular RPMs.
Please keep in mind that this issue is customer-facing.
Customer impact: There are currently 60+ customer cases opened for this issue. Since late Thursday evening, RHEL and Satellite customers are unable to upgrade from RHEL 8 to RHEL 9 and are unable to sync their RHEL 9 repositories. They receive an error: "failed validation due to checksum". There seems to be a workaround for reposync use case, but customer cases are still generated.

comments.author: Daniel Alley
comments.body:
It may not be the case that PQC is even directly relevant, just the fact that these RPMs were republished under the same versions / NEVRA, to the same locations on the CDN, but with different checksums.
If the publish was just a typical "fastforward" publish that appends to the end of the metadata instead of republishing from scratch (assuming that's still how it works, given the changes RHEL-DST has made to Pulp 2), then you'd likely see an error similar to this, because previous references to the package (and the declared checksum) would not have been removed, yet the package would have changed in-place.
So just republishing the builds again may not fix it, unless it does a "force-full (re)publish" to generate all the metadata from scratch.

Regarding the cache:
I reached out to Henning over slack; he mentioned that the cache key for that URL seems to be
X-Cache-Key: S/=/174/67570/30d/cdn.redhat.com/content/dist/rhel9/9/x86_64/appstream/os/Packages/p/pg_repack-1.4.8-2.module+el9.5.0+22224+f5585c78.x86_64.rpm cid=///
He also mentioned that it is possible to obtain the x-cache-key by adding these headers to the request:
-H "Pragma: akamai-x-cache-on, akamai-x-cache-remote-on, akamai-x-check-cacheable, akamai-x-get-cache-key, akamai-x-get-extracted-values, akamai-x-get-nonces, akamai-x-get-ssl-client-session-id, akamai-x-get-true-cache-key, akamai-x-serial-no"
We were attempting to flush an ARL using the "S/=/4177/67570" prefix.
S/=/4177/67570/30d/cdn.redhat.com/content/dist/rhel9/9/x86_64/appstream/os/Packages/p/pg_repack-1.4.8-2.module+el9.5.0+22224+f5585c78.x86_64.rpm cid=///\
But, the X-Cache-Key seems to use the "S/=/174/67570/" prefix:
X-Cache-Key: S/=/174/67570/30d/cdn.redhat.com/content/dist/rhel9/9/x86_64/appstream/os/Packages/p/pg_repack-1.4.8-2.module+el9.5.0+22224+f5585c78.x86_64.rpm cid=///
I checked the X-Cache-Key for all other RPMs that were repushed. They also all use the " S/=/174/67570" prefix. So, it seems that our cache purge ARL templates should be updated to use  S/=/174/67570. Henning mentioned that the prefix could've changed as a result of https://access.redhat.com/articles/cdn_modernization. To update the cache purge ARL templates, I submitted https://gitlab.cee.redhat.com/ansible-playbooks/exodus-gw-playbooks/-/merge_requests/318

comments.author: Caleigh Runge-Hottman
comments.body:
Customer impact: There are currently 60+ customer cases attached to this ticket. Since late Thursday evening, RHEL and Satellite customers are unable to upgrade from https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHEL-8#icft=RHEL-8
 to https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHEL-9#icft=RHEL-9
 and are unable to sync their https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHEL-9#icft=RHEL-9
 repositories. They receive an error: "failed validation due to checksum". There seems to be a workaround for reposync use case, but customer cases are still generated.
Questions: Where in the pipeline does the signing occur? Which team owns or controls the signing of modular RPMs?
Context: We must report (and escalate) a blocking bug to the team that performs the signing of RPMs. Modular RPMs are being resigned with the PQC key, without a version bump. @Clemens Lang stated, "We were very careful to ensure this wouldn't happen for normal RPMs, and I'm honestly not sure why it happens for modular RPMs." We cannot resign new packages under the same NEVRA as old packages. Additionally, any modular RPMs that were previously shipped without PQC signatures and have already been signed with the new PQC signatures (but have not yet been re-shipped) will either need to (1) bump the NVR for the newly signed modular builds or (2) remove the PQC signature from those builds before they can be re-shipped.
Cost/remediation required if the bug is not fixed: We must perform a lengthy remediation process after a resigned modular RPM advisory is shipped. The duration of the remediation process (which is simply a work around to cover up a large problem) varies based on how many repositories are affected, the size of the repositories, the current load on pub, and whether another engineer is available in another timezone for hand-off. The first "clean up" took roughly 44 hours (over the weekend), the second "clean up" took 40 hours, and the third "clean up" is ongoing. As soon as we perform one "clean up", another modular RPM is shipped (which again breaks the sync and upgrade feature, extending the outage). To avoid performing this remediation process yet again, we will not ship any modular RPM advisories until the underlying bug is fixed.

comments.author: Caleigh Runge-Hottman
comments.body:
This Jira ticket's immediate purpose is complete: the customer escalations reported over the past 1.5 weeks are now considered resolved. Immediate fixes have been deployed to mitigate current customer impact. However, it is important to note that until the final long-term solution for Issue 1 is fully implemented, the potential for similar, future customer escalations remains. 

Issue 1: Component RPM Resigning and NVR Conflict
- Real Root Cause: The core issue was that some component RPMs within a module, whose content had not changed, were resigned with new PQC signatures. Because the component RPMs (which had already been shipped to several previous RHEL versions) retained their original NVRs, this created duplicates (PQC-signed and non-PQC-signed versions with the same NVR) in RHEL <9.7 repositories. 

- Resolution:
- Immediate Fixes/Cleanup (DONE): The duplicate modular RPMs were initially addressed by RHELDST through manual cleanup (described in earlier comments in this ticket). This is a long manual process, often requiring 40+ hours per advisory, with customers unable to access the content while the cleanup is underway.

- Next Steps:
- RHEL Engineering (IN PROGRESS): Modular RPMs that have been signed with the new PQC signatures (including both modules that have been shipped in the last 1.5 weeks and modules that are currently in the Errata workflow) must undergo a full module rebuild. RHEL engineering will rebuild the affected modules.

- RHELDST (IN PROGRESS):  Ship the rebuilt modules.

- RHELDST (TODO): Perform additional manual clean-up. (Cannot do until the modules that were shipped in the last 1.5 weeks have been rebuilt and shipped.)

- Put a temporary workaround in place so we can ship modules safely until the proper long-term fix is implemented AND reduce manual interventions to expedite releases.

- RHELDST (TODO): Resume release-driver automation. (Cannot do until a temporary workaround is in place.)


- Long-Term Solution (TODO): The PQC experts/Working Group will implement a proper long-term module-handling solution to permanently prevent this issue.


Issue 2: Caching Case-Sensitivity of Encoded URLs
- Root Cause: The underlying caching issue was due to the Akamai cache flush being case-sensitive regarding percent-encoded URLs. The initial troubleshooting was tracked in this issue (RHELDST-37695), in which the cache flushing issue was partially identified. The error messages reported being unable to fetch content from uppercase percent-encoded URLs (e.g., %2B). Despite repeated cache flushing attempts of two variations of the URLs (non-encoded and uppercase percent-encoded), the cache flushing attempts only fixed direct downloads of the content (e.g., downloading of content from non-encoded and uppercase percent-encoded URLs directly using curl), but failed to fix downloads using reposync. This led to the filing of TEAMNADO-9077, in which Teamnado discovered that while error logs contained uppercase percent-encoded URLs, dnfwas actually fetching content from the lowercase variant (%2b ). Since the cache flush was case-sensitive, content remained stale. 

- Why was this cache flushing quirk previously unknown? Static, immutable artifacts do not require cache flushes. Mutable artifacts on the CDN (e.g., repository metadata) do not contain URLs with special characters that would change the URL when encoded. RPMs are considered static, immutable artifacts; a RPM shipped to a path on the CDN should not change, and thus wouldn’t typically require a cache flush. Module NVRs contain special characters (e.g., “+”).

- Resolution/Final Actions:
- Immediate Fixes/Cleanup (DONE): RHELDST flushed the cache (all URL variants) for all of the error-causing modules that were shipped in the last 1.5 weeks.

- Long-Term Solution (DONE): The cache flushing mechanism has been permanently modified (documented in RHELDST-37769). It now explicitly flushes all URL variants; it flushes paths containing +, and both lowercase (%2b  ) and uppercase (%2B ) percent-encoded URLs. This modification ensures correct cache behavior for future module clean-up (if/when needed).



The customer impact from the reported escalations has been mitigated, and a permanent solution for Issue 2 is in place. Given that the immediate fixes for Issue 1 are defined and additional remediation is underway, the ticket can now be closed from an active customer escalation standpoint.

RHELDST-38946.description:
After we finish https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHELDST-37824
  , any attempt of upload of duplicated RPM to rhsm-pulp will result in fatal error and currently it’s not known how to remediate such problem (or at least there is not any widely agreed procedure).  
Because the raised error would be the last possible measure before reaching CDN the problem should likely be remediated in previous parts of release pipeline (e.g. by re-building RPM and bumping NVR). Note that this error would block the push completely until problem is resolved. 
Propose a remediation procedure for such situations which will be easily applicable for our ticketmasters/releng.

Acceptance criteria:
-  there is known and agreed procedure for remediating attempted upload of duplicated RPM
- procedure is documented in https://redhat.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/RHELDST/pages/175375939/Ticket+Handling
